page: Amazon Web Services m4.xlarge is a fourth-generation general-purpose virtual machine based on the Xen hypervisor. Powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 Broadwell processor clocked at 2.4 GHz, the instance provides 4 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 2 physical cores with hyperthreading enabled. It is configured with 16.0 GB of system memory, maintaining a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4.0 GB per virtual core. The instance includes a 45 MB L3 cache, standard AVX vector extensions, and hardware AES cryptographic acceleration, though it lacks modern instruction sets such as AVX-512 or AMX.

The hardware configuration includes no bundled local storage, requiring network-attached Elastic Block Store volumes for operational persistence. In addition, no discrete GPUs are attached, and baseline network throughput is rated at 1 Gbps. In benchmark evaluations, the m4.xlarge consistently scores within the lower tiers. Geekbench results register a single-core score of 976.0 and a multi-core score of 2156.0, while Passmark CPU and memory tests place overall execution and bandwidth capabilities in the lower 25th percentile. Memory throughput reaches 24.01 GB/s on large unbuffered reads and 21.65 GB/s on writes.

Due to its legacy hardware profile, the instance exhibits modest throughput across standard operational workloads, achieving 1.44 million Redis SET operations per second and 3.36 GB/s in static web serving throughput. From an infrastructure cost perspective, this generation offers diminished computational density and power efficiency compared to newer architectures, meaning that cost efficiency is lower unless deployed under specific legacy software compatibility requirements. The m4.xlarge is suited primarily for standard general-purpose tasks such as small-scale application servers, low-concurrency web backends, dev-test environments, and internal tracking utilities that do not require high I/O throughput or advanced instruction sets.
description: Amazon Web Services m4.xlarge is a fourth-generation general-purpose instance featuring 4 dedicated vCPUs and 16.0 GB of RAM. Driven by an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor operating at 2.4 GHz on the Xen hypervisor, it provides 2 physical cores with 2 threads per core alongside a balanced 1:4 compute-to-memory ratio. The instance includes no local storage or GPUs, relying on network-attached storage and a 1 Gbps baseline network interface. In benchmark assessments, including Geekbench and Passmark, the older Broadwell architecture yields performance metrics largely in the lower 25th percentile, reflecting reduced compute density relative to contemporary hardware. Consequently, qualitative cost efficiency is modest, positioning the m4.xlarge as an entry-level general-purpose compute node for legacy workloads, non-critical web serving, development testing, and moderate enterprise background tasks.
